table.caption: Plant species and above-ground plant biomass in fields of different ages since farming stopped, one region (invented data for practice)

succession-s2.title: Life returns to a volcano
succession-s2.passage: In May 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted. The blast flattened 600 square kilometers of forest, and a fan of hot rock and ash on the volcano’s north side, later named the Pumice Plain, buried the ground under many meters of fresh rock. On the Pumice Plain, nothing survived; a few years later only scattered plants had arrived. Farther out, where the blast knocked trees down but left soil, roots and buried seeds, plants sprouted the first summer, and pocket gophers dug fresh soil up to the surface. Ecologists who have studied both areas since 1980 report that life returned much faster where soil remained than on the rock of the Pumice Plain.
succession-s2.source: Invented passage for practice, summarizing USGS accounts and published research at Mount St. Helens.

items.q: Which statement best describes how plant biomass changes as the fields age?
options: It increases throughout, from 0.4 to 30.0 kg per m²
It rises for 60 years, then falls to its starting level
It stays near 1 kg per m² throughout
It falls as larger plants shade out the weeds

why.correct: Give the direction and the start and end values.
options: Right: biomass rises at every step, most of all as trees take over.
Biomass is higher at 150 years (30.0) than at 60 (18.0).
It reaches 30.0 kg per m² by 150 years.
Larger plants add biomass; the total rises.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in the number of plant species from the 1-year field to the 20-year field, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: That divides by 38. Divide by the starting value, 12.
That is the change in species. Divide by 12 and multiply by 100.
Divide by the starting value, 12 species in the 1-year field, not by 38.
Without brackets the division happens first. Write (38 - 12) / 12 × 100.

items.q: What kind of succession do these fields show, and why?
options: Primary, because the fields began with no plants growing
Secondary, because soil remained when farming stopped
Primary, because weeds are pioneer species
Secondary, because the fields began as bare rock

why.correct: The key question is whether soil was present at the start.
options: Primary succession needs no soil; these fields had soil.
Right: an abandoned field keeps its soil and seeds, so succession is secondary.
Pioneer species appear in both kinds; the starting soil decides the kind.
Bare rock would make it primary, and these fields had soil.

items.q: Species richness falls slightly from 45 at 60 years to 42 at 150 years while biomass keeps rising. Which explanation fits succession best?
options: The soil runs out of nutrients after about 60 years
Pioneer species return and crowd out the oaks
Tall oaks shade out some sun-loving species
Biomass and richness rise and fall together

why.correct: Richness often peaks in the middle stages, when early and late species overlap.
options: Biomass keeps rising, so the soil still supports more plant growth.
Oaks and hickories are most common at 150 years.
Right: in a mature forest a few large trees dominate and shade out some plants that need light.
They do not here: biomass rises while richness dips.

items.q: Which claim does the passage support?
options: The eruption killed each plant across 600 square kilometers
Pocket gophers caused the eruption by digging
The Pumice Plain recovered first because it was closest
Life returned faster where soil remained

why.correct: The passage compares the two areas and states which recovered faster.
options: Plants sprouted the first summer where soil, roots and seeds survived.
Gophers dug soil after the eruption; they did not cause it.
The passage says the Pumice Plain recovered slowly.
Right: plants sprouted the first summer where soil remained, but slowly on the Pumice Plain.

items.q: Which detail from the passage best supports calling the Pumice Plain an example of primary succession?
options: It was buried under fresh rock, with nothing surviving
It lies on the north side of the volcano, facing the blast
It covers part of the 600 square kilometers of flattened forest
It was given its name by scientists after the eruption

why.correct: Primary succession starts with no soil and no surviving organisms.
options: Right: no soil and no surviving life is the starting point of primary succession.
The direction does not decide the kind of succession.
The size does not decide the kind of succession.
A name does not show anything about soil.

items.q: Pocket gophers survived underground and dug old soil up onto the new ash. How would this most likely affect plants in those areas?
options: It slows plant growth by burying the seeds deeper
It speeds plant growth by bringing up soil with nutrients and seeds
It has no effect, because ash and soil are the same
It stops succession, because gophers eat the young plants

why.correct: Anything that brings back soil, seeds or nutrients makes succession faster.
options: The gophers brought soil up, not down.
Right: mixing old soil into the ash gives plants nutrients, water storage and buried seeds.
Fresh ash lacks the nutrients and organisms of old soil.
Gophers eat some plants, but bringing soil up helps more plants grow.

items.q: Which of these sites would undergo primary succession?
options: A forest after a wildfire
A cornfield that is no longer farmed
Rock bared by a melting glacier
A floodplain after a spring flood

why.correct: Primary succession starts on surfaces with no soil.
options: Soil remains after a fire, so that is secondary succession.
An old field keeps its soil, so that is secondary succession.
Right: the glacier scraped the land to bare rock with no soil.
Floods leave soil, often adding more, so that is secondary.

items.q: Lichens are often the first organisms on bare rock. How do they help other species follow?
options: They shade the rock so no other species can grow
They eat the seeds of other plants that arrive
They raise the rock’s temperature so trees can grow at once
They weather rock and add dead matter, forming soil

why.correct: Pioneer species change the site so that later species can live there.
options: Lichens are tiny and do not block other species; they make room for them.
Lichens do not eat seeds; they make their food by photosynthesis.
Trees need soil, which takes a long time to form.
Right: lichens release acids that weather rock, and their remains add organic matter, the start of soil.

items.q: Put the stages of primary succession on a new lava flow in order, from first to last.
options: Bare rock with no soil
Lichens and mosses colonize the rock
Grasses and small plants grow in thin soil
Shrubs and fast-growing trees take over
A mature forest develops

why.correct: Rock, then pioneers that start soil, then plants that need soil, then shrubs and trees, then a mature community.

items.q: Which changes usually happen as succession moves toward a mature community? Select all that apply.
options: Total biomass decreases as trees replace grasses
Soil becomes deeper and richer
Pioneer species become more common
The community becomes less stable

why.correct: Succession builds soil and biomass, replaces pioneers with longer-lived species, and makes the community more stable. Only the soil statement is correct.
options: Trees are larger and longer-lived than grasses, so total biomass increases.
Right: plants and decomposers add organic matter to the soil.
Pioneers are replaced by later species as conditions change.
Mature communities are usually more stable.

items.q: A hurricane knocks down most of the trees in a coastal forest but leaves the soil in place. Which description of what follows is correct?
options: Secondary, starting with fast-growing plants
Primary, starting with lichens and mosses on bare rock
No succession, because the forest was already mature
Primary, because most of the trees were destroyed

why.correct: Secondary succession follows any disruption that leaves soil.
options: Right: soil remains, so it is secondary, and sun-loving pioneers grow first in the gaps.
There is no bare rock; the soil is still there.
The disruption resets the community, so succession begins again.
What decides primary or secondary is the soil, not the trees.

items.q: Explain why secondary succession is faster than primary succession.

why.correct: Name what secondary succession starts with, what primary succession must do first, and the result.

specific.frame: In secondary succession, ___ are already present, while primary succession must first ___, so ___.

cause.label: What remains
options: soil, seeds and roots
large mature trees
bare rock and ash

why.1: Mature trees are usually removed by the disruption.
why.2: Bare rock is the start of primary succession, not secondary.

effect.label: Extra step in primary
options: build soil from bare rock, which takes centuries
wait for a fire to clear the land
remove the soil that is already there

why.1: Primary succession does not need a fire; it needs soil.
why.2: There is no soil to remove in primary succession.

mechanism.label: Result
options: plants can grow sooner in secondary succession
primary succession reaches a mature forest first
both take the same time

why.1: Primary succession is slower because soil must form first.
why.2: Building soil adds a long first step to primary succession.

specific.model: In secondary succession, soil, seeds and roots are already present, while primary succession must first build soil from bare rock, which takes centuries, so plants can grow sooner in secondary succession.

items.q: A town plans to let an old parking lot become a natural meadow by removing the pavement and gravel down to bare, packed ground and leaving it alone. Which advice is best supported by succession?
options: Leaving the ground bare is fastest, because pioneers come anyway
Adding soil and native seed would speed recovery
Planting mature oak trees first will give a meadow at once
Covering the site with gravel again will help plants root

why.correct: The slow step is building soil; supplying soil and seeds speeds succession.
options: Pioneers will come, but poor soil makes the early stages slow.
Right: adding soil and seeds skips the slow early stages.
Oaks are late-stage plants; they do not make a meadow and grow poorly in bare, packed ground.
Gravel blocks soil formation and makes plant growth harder.

items.q: A pond slowly fills with sediment and dead plants over hundreds of years, becoming a marsh and later a meadow. Which idea from this topic does this show?
options: A periodic disruption that returns each spring
Island biogeography, as the pond is an isolated habitat
Succession, as the community changes in stages
Natural selection, as pond animals change their traits

why.correct: Any gradual replacement of one community by another in stages is succession.
options: Filling over centuries is a slow change, not a yearly event.
The pond is changing into a different community; that is succession.
Right: the community changes in a series of stages as the site itself changes.
The species present change, not the traits of one species.
